The ABCs of Landlording - A Five-Minute Masterclass

Landlording is not a hobby you fall into and hope for the best, it is a business you either run with discipline or let run you ragged. The core promise here is simple, treat the property like a company with systems and numbers, not like a favor you are doing for whoever knocks on the door, and it will pay you steadily instead of draining you unpredictably.

1. Screen every applicant the same way, every time. Run credit, verify income at 3 times the rent, check past landlords, and confirm employment before you ever hand over a key. Skipping this step for a tenant who seems nice is how good landlords end up with 6 months of unpaid rent and an eviction file.

2. Put everything in the lease, nothing in a handshake. Your lease should spell out rent due dates, late fees, who handles what repair, pet rules, and grounds for termination in plain language. If a dispute ever lands in front of a judge, the lease is the only thing that speaks for you, so write it like you expect to need it.

3. Price rent to the market, not to your emotions. Check what comparable units in your area actually rent for every year and adjust accordingly, even if it feels awkward to raise a good tenant's rent. Underpricing out of guilt is a quiet way to lose thousands of dollars a year while your costs keep climbing.

4. Collect rent on a fixed schedule and enforce it without exception. Set one due date, a short grace period, and a real late fee, then apply the same rule to every tenant regardless of their story. The moment you bend the rule for one person, you have taught everyone that your rules are optional.

5. Respond to maintenance requests fast, especially the urgent ones. A leaking pipe or broken heater ignored for a week turns into a much bigger repair bill and a tenant who stops trusting you enough to pay on time. Fast, competent repairs are one of the cheapest ways to keep good tenants and protect your property's value.

6. Keep a cash reserve separate from your regular income. Set aside 3 to 6 months of expenses per property for vacancies, emergency repairs, and slow months, and never treat rent income as spending money the day it lands. Landlords who skip this step get forced into bad decisions the first time a furnace dies in January.

7. Document every interaction, inspection, and repair in writing. Photograph the unit at move in and move out, keep receipts for every repair, and put notices in writing with dates. When a dispute happens, and eventually one will, the landlord with a paper trail wins and the one relying on memory loses.

8. Learn the landlord tenant law in your state before you need it. Know the legal notice periods, the rules for security deposits, and the exact eviction process, because guessing wrong can cost you the case and the money.

9. Separate the person from the business when you make decisions. Being firm about rent and rules is not cruelty, it is what keeps the property solvent enough to house anyone at all, so make decisions based on the lease and the numbers, not on sympathy in the moment. You can be kind and still say no.

10. Build systems so the business does not depend entirely on you. Use a written process for turnovers, a standard maintenance vendor list, and a simple bookkeeping method you update monthly, so someone else could step in and understand your operation. Landlords who keep everything in their head burn out or make expensive mistakes when life gets busy.

11. Review your numbers every year like a business owner would. Look at your actual cash flow after taxes, insurance, vacancy, and repairs, not just the rent check, and decide whether each property still earns its place in your portfolio. A property that only looks profitable because you never did the math is not actually profitable.

Every one of these principles points back to the same idea, a rental property rewards the owner who runs it like a business and punishes the owner who runs it on hope. Screen carefully, write it down, price it honestly, collect on schedule, fix it fast, and keep a reserve for the day something breaks. Do those things consistently and landlording stops being a source of stress and starts being what it was always supposed to be, a steady, well managed source of income.
